questions.learningObjective: Explain how the 1935 act reached elderly residents with no income.
questions.stem: A welfare survey records elderly residents of one county with no income of their own, and you must explain how federal policy began to reach them. Write a short account of the 1935 act's approach.

answer.exemplar: The Social Security Act of 1935 created an old-age insurance system funded by payroll contributions from employers and workers, with benefits paid to retired workers and their dependents, plus survivor and disability benefits and aid to the aged. It also set up a separate federal and state program of assistance for needy people too old to work. Because the aged often had no wages and no savings, the survey's households could not be reached by ordinary relief programs alone, and the new law supplied an income where none existed.

questions.explanation: The 1935 act used payroll financed old-age insurance plus a separate assistance program for the aged, which is how it reached households with no income. The survey asks for the policy's design, not its reception.
questions.hint: Consider whether aid was funded by payroll taxes or by relief.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how deposit insurance changed depositor behavior.
questions.stem: A survey of the county's surviving savings banks records that their deposits grew steadily through the 1930s while nearby commercial banks failed. Write a short account of the change the new law made.

answer.exemplar: Federal deposit insurance changed the response to a rumor of failure. Before it, a depositor who heard that a bank was in trouble had every reason to withdraw first, and the withdrawals in turn emptied the bank and made the rumor true. Once insured accounts could be repaid at another institution, the motive to rush disappeared for most small depositors, and the survey area's stable banks gained deposits that panicked ones had lost. The law did not create savings; it removed the reason to run for them.

questions.explanation: Insurance removed the motive to run, because depositors knew they would be repaid elsewhere, which is why the surveyed banks held their deposits. The question asks what the law changed, not who lobbied for it.
questions.hint: Ask what a depositor's reason for withdrawing first was.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the sequence of events that produced the 1929 market collapse.
questions.stem: Guided through a brokerage's abandoned floor, a local historian asks why the crowd outside fell so sharply in late October 1929. Write a short account of the sequence of events.

answer.exemplar: The fall was a sequence rather than a single cause. Prices had been carried by buying financed with borrowed money, so the market's strength depended on confidence about tomorrow's price. When a visible warning appeared that the speculation had gone too far, brokers demanded more collateral from the least secure accounts, and those accounts sold whether they wished to or not. The selling met thin buying, prices fell, the fall made the margin calls worse, and the process fed itself until the crowd outside the exchange had thinned to a few onlookers.

questions.explanation: The crash unfolded as borrowing, calls, forced selling, and falling prices reinforced one another over several sessions. The account asks for that sequence, not for a single culprit.
questions.hint: Ask what happened between the margin call and the next fall.

What we have not been told is who will build the schools, or whether the trolleys will run the last three miles of the road that now separates the suburbs from the city we all still use for work.

questions.stem: The editors' letter in your survey archive raises a question the numbers do not answer. Which concern is best supported?

options.text: That the suburbs would eventually replace the city entirely, since the letter predicts the end of the city as a place of work.
options.misconception: Belief that the letter predicts the end of the city.

options.text: That the housing program was a failure, since the letter shows that veterans received no houses at all in the new developments.
options.misconception: Belief that the letter shows veterans received no houses.

options.text: That the local banks opposed the program, since the lenders' role in the letter suggests they had refused to make loans.
options.misconception: Belief that the lenders' role shows they refused to lend.

options.text: That new housing policy delivered houses while leaving schools, transport, and employment centers behind, which residents felt keenly.

questions.explanation: The letter notes what the new housing supplied and what it did not, namely schools, transport, and jobs still downtown. Believing the program delivered nothing, that lenders refused to lend, or that it dooms the city overreads it.
questions.hint: Ask what the letter says was missing from the new suburbs.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how margin calls turned a fall into a collapse.
questions.stem: Your survey of a trading district records a session in which share prices fell 40 percent in a single afternoon. Which account best explains how a good day of trading turned so fast?

options.text: Exchange officials lowered the price of every listed stock at once, so the fall came from a single administrative decision.
options.misconception: Belief that officials reset all prices at once.

options.text: Buyers who had borrowed against rising prices were told to cover their loans at the new prices, and their sales drove the decline further.
The day's trading was cancelled early, and the recorded figure came from the last few trades before the halt.
options.misconception: Belief that the figure came from a short session.

options.text: A single industrial company failed at midday, and every other stock fell because it had been sold shares of that company.
options.misconception: Belief that one failure sank the whole market at once.

questions.explanation: Margin calls at falling prices forced selling into a thin market, so the decline reinforced itself within hours. Believing officials reset prices or that trading was halted misreads the sequence.
questions.hint: Ask what a falling price does to a borrowed position.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a depositor run from bank record data.
questions.stem: A review of county bank records shows deposits falling 40 percent in a week at three institutions, county officials praising the same banks as sound a month earlier, and each of the three buildings later sold at auction. Which reading is best supported?

options.text: The withdrawals show the state had already suspended the banks, since regulators close banks before deposits leave.
options.misconception: Belief that regulators closed the banks before the runs.

options.text: The withdrawals show the banks were sound, since customers moved their money only when they found a safer bank.
options.misconception: Belief that heavy withdrawals prove a bank's soundness.

options.text: The withdrawals point to a depositor run, in which confidence rather than solvency emptied the banks and forced their sale.
The withdrawals show the banks held no deposits at all, since customers had quietly emptied them years before.
options.misconception: Belief that the banks had been empty for years.

questions.explanation: A 40 percent fall in deposits within a week, after praise of the banks, marks a confidence run, and the auction sales follow the failure. Believing it shows soundness or prior suspension contradicts the record.
questions.hint: Ask what a one week collapse in deposits is called.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what automatic benefit payments changed for county relief work.
questions.stem: A county welfare survey turns up beneficiaries whose checks arrived by post without an application, and your notes must explain what that arrangement meant for the county. Write a short account.

answer.exemplar: Checks that arrived by post without an application changed the county's relief work in two ways. The aged no longer had to be found and investigated one case at a time, which freed caseworkers from repeated visits and home checks. And because the payment was automatic, an elderly resident did not have to show public need to anyone before receiving it, which removed the humiliation that had accompanied relief in the surveyed county and steadied the household's income from month to month.

questions.explanation: Automatic payments by post removed the search, the investigation, and the public need test from the county's relief work. The account asks what the arrangement changed for the county and the recipient.
questions.hint: Ask what work the county no longer had to do.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Deficit spending in the New Deal
questions.learningObjective: Explain why federal spending produced uneven results across counties.
questions.stem: Your survey route passes a state highway project and a county whose relief rolls grew for three years despite federal spending elsewhere. Which reasoning about deficit spending best fits the record?

options.text: The federal program should have been ended, since results that vary from county to county show it had no useful effect anywhere.
options.misconception: Belief that uneven results mean a program has no effect.

options.text: The county must have wasted its share, since federal spending always produces lower relief rolls wherever it arrives.
options.misconception: Belief that federal spending always lowers relief rolls.

options.text: The county must have received no funds at all, since relief rolls rose, which shows the federal program had no presence in the state.
options.misconception: Belief that rising relief rolls prove no funds arrived.

options.text: Spending effects depend on where the money is spent and what it produces, so the same program can relieve one county and leave another strained.

questions.explanation: Public spending is not self executing, since a road or a wage differs by county and labor market. Believing the results mean waste, that no funds arrived, or that variation voids a program confuses variation for failure.
questions.hint: Ask what the county's economy could absorb.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Assess a regulatory order that combines procedure with a legal objection.

stimulus.body: The order set a schedule of maximum charges for the service, required the company to keep its rates on file with the commission, and provided that any complaint about the service be heard at a stated time and place. A dissenting opinion observed that the company had entered the business on its own account, that its risks were its own, and that nothing in the record showed the public had been harmed by the charges in question.

questions.stem: The regulatory order in your survey files combines administrative practice with a legal objection. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The order shows the commission had found the company guilty of overcharging, since a maximum charge was imposed on it.
options.misconception: Belief that a maximum charge proves a finding of overcharging.

options.text: The order created enforceable procedures for rate control while the objection rested on the freedom of the business to set its terms.
The order shows the rates were fixed by the company's competitors, since the schedule had to be kept on file with the commission.
options.misconception: Belief that competitors set the rates in the schedule.

options.text: The order shows the commission lacked jurisdiction, since the dissent observed that no harm to the public had been shown.
options.misconception: Belief that the dissent proves the commission lacked jurisdiction.

questions.explanation: The order sets procedures for control while the objection denies the public harm that would justify it. Believing it found wrongdoing, that competitors set rates, or that jurisdiction failed overreads it.
questions.hint: Ask what the order required and what the objection disputed.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize the long-term effects of farm depopulation on a county.
questions.stem: A roadside survey of the plains records a county that lost farms faster than it gained them, and you must synthesize what the pattern says about the region's long-term economy. Which reading is best?

options.text: Depopulation ended the county's problems, since the schools and roads that had burdened the tax base closed with the families.
options.misconception: Belief that fewer residents automatically closed the burden.

options.text: Depopulation concentrated ownership, so the remaining farms became larger and more productive without any loss to the community.
options.misconception: Belief that fewer farms always meant a stronger local economy.

options.text: Depopulation thinned the tax base and the labor supply, so the county's remaining institutions grew harder to sustain as the farms went.
Depopulation was temporary, since the survey shows families returning to the county within a single season.
options.misconception: Belief that the survey shows families returning within a season.

questions.explanation: Losing farms meant losing taxpayers, workers, and students, which raised the cost of running what remained. Believing concentration was costless, that depopulation solved the budget, or that families returned quickly misreads the pattern.
questions.hint: Ask what left the county along with the families.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features of directed war production conversion.
questions.stem: Reviewing plant ledgers, you find civilian production cut by half while war orders multiplied, and a note that the plant was directed to retool. Which feature of war production conversion is best illustrated?

options.text: Production was shifted by accident, since the plant was converted when the civilian market disappeared without any decision.
options.misconception: Belief that the conversion happened without a decision.

options.text: Production was shifted by market forces, since buyers simply preferred tanks to farm machinery and the plant followed demand.
options.misconception: Belief that civilian producers switched because buyers preferred war goods.

options.text: Production was shifted by labor shortage, since the plant could not find the workers to keep making civilian goods.
options.misconception: Belief that a labor shortage forced the switch to war orders.

options.text: Production was shifted by federal direction, so civilian output fell while military orders rose under the same roof and labor force.

questions.explanation: The retooling order shows conversion was directed from outside the firm, which distinguished it from an ordinary market shift. Believing preference, shortage, or accident caused it misreads the direction of the change.
questions.hint: Ask who decided what the plant would make.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret loan guarantee figures and their effect on homeownership.
questions.stem: Tallying building permits in a postwar suburb, you find that 4.3 million home loans were backed by federal guarantees, that most new houses stood on land outside the central cities, and that the guaranteed loans went to buyers with modest savings. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The guarantees raised the number of people living in the central cities, since buyers preferred to stay near their work.
options.misconception: Belief that the guarantees increased central city population.

options.text: Federal guarantees moved ownership outward from the central cities, making suburban home purchase possible for families with modest means.
The guarantees raised house prices beyond reach, since the lenders charged the market rate on every guaranteed loan.
options.misconception: Belief that guaranteed loans were priced at the market rate.

options.text: The guarantees served only the wealthiest buyers, since modest savers could not meet the terms of the loans.
options.misconception: Belief that only the wealthiest could use the guarantees.

questions.explanation: Guarantees made lending to buyers with modest savings possible, and most new building stood outside the central cities, so ownership moved outward. Believing they raised city populations, or served only the wealthy, misreads them.
questions.hint: Ask where the new houses went and who could buy them.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why brokers insisted on margin deposits.
questions.stem: Surveying a brokerage ruin, you find a ledger showing that investors bought stock with a small cash deposit. Which reasoning best explains why brokers insisted on that arrangement?

options.text: The small deposit reduced the buyer's risk, since the broker absorbed any loss beyond the amount actually paid.
options.misconception: Belief that brokers absorbed losses beyond the deposit.

options.text: The small deposit let brokers lend more money to more customers, which was the arrangement's chief purpose.
options.misconception: Belief that the arrangement existed to expand broker lending.

options.text: The small deposit let a buyer control a much larger share of stock, so a modest change in price produced a large gain or loss.
The small deposit was a legal requirement, so brokers could not accept full payment for listed shares.
options.misconception: Belief that margin buying was required by law.

questions.explanation: Small deposits magnified the effect of price changes on the buyer's capital, which drew investors to the arrangement. Believing it was a lending scheme or a risk transfer misreads the mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask what a small deposit buys in terms of stock.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the mechanism by which a bank run begins.
questions.stem: Surveying the site of a collapsed bank, you must explain why depositors rushed to withdraw their money in the first place. Write a short account of the mechanism.

answer.exemplar: Depositors ran because they had no reason to wait and every reason to move first. A bank holds only a fraction of its deposits in cash, keeping most of the money out on loans, so a demand for withdrawals has to be met by calling loans back or by selling securities at a loss. If a rumor suggested the bank was weak, the depositor who withdrew that day was protected while the one who waited risked finding a closed door, and the expectations of a run became self fulfilling.

questions.explanation: A bank holds only part of its deposits in cash, so one depositor's fear becomes everyone's risk, which turned a rumor into a run. The account asks for the mechanism, not the outcome.
questions.hint: Ask what a bank keeps on hand and what it has lent out.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize why entitlement payments protected the poorest elderly residents.
questions.stem: A retirement survey in one county finds that payments arrived based on work history rather than on a local decision, and asks you to synthesize what that means for the county's poorest residents. Which reading is best?

options.text: Payments by right are inadequate, because an automatic monthly sum cannot cover the housing costs that relief grants had once met.
options.misconception: Belief that automatic benefits cannot cover housing costs.

options.text: Payments by right are unfair, because residents who never worked in covered employment now receive the same benefit as those who did.
options.misconception: Belief that a work record makes unequal treatment unfair.

options.text: Payments by right are irrelevant, since the county's own relief program continued to set the living standard of its poorest residents.
options.misconception: Belief that local relief still set the poorest standard.

options.text: Regular income by right protects elderly residents better than discretionary relief, because no official's judgment decides whether they eat.

questions.explanation: An automatic entitlement removes the discretion that made relief unpredictable for the poorest elderly. Believing the work record is unfair, that relief still set the standard, or that the sum was too small misses the point.
questions.hint: Ask what the recipient no longer had to prove.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Deficit spending in the New Deal
questions.learningObjective: Assess the stated purposes of a federal works program.

stimulus.body: The notice informed state authorities that the program of public works would be continued through the following year, and that payments for completed projects would be made on a schedule rather than on demand, since the federal office had committed funds to wages already paid. It noted that the works program was intended to give employment to men who had no other work, and that the projects themselves would be judged by whether they added to the useful infrastructure of the area.

questions.stem: The works notice in your survey files explains the logic of a relief program. Which conclusion does it best support?

options.text: The program was primarily a banking program, since payments made on a schedule were the same as loans to state authorities.
options.misconception: Belief that scheduled payments make the program a lending scheme.

options.text: The program was framed as employment for men without work, with the projects judged by what they added to local infrastructure.
The program was intended to reduce government spending, since works done by the states instead of the federal government cost less.
options.misconception: Belief that the program was a plan to reduce government spending.

options.text: The program was a private enterprise scheme, since the notice describes payments for completed projects rather than public work.
options.misconception: Belief that payments for projects make the program private.

questions.explanation: The notice frames the program as employment for the jobless, with projects judged by the infrastructure they added. Believing it was lending, a cost cutting scheme, or private enterprise misreads the stated purpose.
questions.hint: Ask whom the program was meant to employ and what to build.
